Big Question
Today’s Wonder

Lamb keeps a crowded island clear: which lord was kind, which son leaped first. How do a few words between commas do that?

✏️ Daily Oral Language

An appositive in the middle of a sentence takes a comma on both sides.

🔧 Fix this one
ferdinand the kings son carried heavy logs for prospero
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

Ferdinand, the king’s son, carried heavy logs for Prospero. Both names take a capital letter. The king’s son renames Ferdinand, so it sits between two commas, and the apostrophe shows that the son belongs to the king. A pair of dashes around the king’s son would also be correct.

🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Professor Lovelore At the board
0:40
An AI-generated character and voice.
Appositive
A noun beside a noun, renaming it.
An example
Gonzalo, a kind lord, packed the boat.
a kind lord→renames Gonzalo
Lift it out
Gonzalo packed the boat.
A whole sentence is still left.
Where the commas go
Middle: two commas.
End: one comma.
Prospero thanked Gonzalo, a kind lord.
Dashes
A list inside, or a big reveal? Dashes: a pair, or one at the end.
The twins—Sam and Kai—won the race.
In Lamb’s tale
Lamb: commas, and (parentheses) for asides.
No dashes in this tale.

✏️ Grammar: Learn the Labels
Step 1 of 4

Pick a label, then tap the word or group it belongs to. A label can be used more than once.

LabelWhat it doesExample
subject nounnames who or what does the actionThe boat drifted.
verbwhat is being said about the subjectThe boat drifted.
appositivea noun, or a group of words around a noun, beside another noun, renaming itThe boat, a tiny craft, drifted.
Theking’sship,a fine large vessel,laysafeintheharbor.
Which noun does a fine large vessel rename?
Prospero’senemies—the king of Naples and Antonio—landedontheisland.
Why does this appositive sit between dashes?
Four ways to set it off
  1. Middle: two commas Gonzalo, a kind lord, packed the boat.
  2. End: one comma Prospero thanked Gonzalo, a kind lord.
  3. Dashes: a pair, or one at the end Prospero’s enemies—the king and Antonio—landed.Use them when the appositive holds a list or a pair of names, or when you want it to land hard.
  4. Parentheses: a quiet aside Lamb uses them often. What sits inside is not always an appositive.

🗂️ Grammar: Sort Them
Step 3 of 4: sort twelve sentences.
Miranda, Prospero’s only heir, begged him to save the ship. Two men—the king of Naples and Antonio—had wronged Prospero. Miranda, who had seen no man but her father, thought Ferdinand was a spirit. The storm threw Antonio, Prospero’s younger brother, onto the island. When the storm ended, every sailor was safe. Gonzalo packed four things—water, food, clothes, and books—into the boat. Prospero raised the storm with Ariel, the chief of his spirits. Ferdinand’s task—the job of piling logs—was really a test. Ferdinand drew his sword, but Prospero froze him with his wand. Sycorax, a witch from Algiers, had shut Ariel in a tree. In place of the banquet stood one creature—a harpy. Prospero smiled and nodded his head.
Appositive, set off with commas

Gonzalo helped in secret. What does that tell you about Milan after Antonio took power?

✏️ Read like a Writer

Prospero names the helper last: a kind lord of my court, one Gonzalo. The appositive one Gonzalo renames a kind lord. Why might he save the name for after the kindness?

✏️ Make a Word Your Own

Pick one of the ten words. Lamb’s line appears. Then work it three ways.

Swap

Replace the word with a word that means almost the same. Does the meaning shift?

Stretch

Keep the word. Add detail until the picture is sharper.

Imitate

Keep the shape of the sentence. Write about your own life.

Which is strongest?

Pick your strongest version and say why.

Jonah
6th Grade Scholar · a model
Lamb “He followed in amazement the sound of Ariel's voice” Word: amazement
Swap He followed in wonder the sound of Ariel’s voice.
Stretch Ferdinand, still wet from the sea, followed in amazement the sound of Ariel’s voice across the grass.
Imitate I followed in amazement the sound of the ice-cream truck down our street.
Best The stretch, because you can see him dripping and confused.

Revenge or Forgiveness? When someone has wronged you and you could get even, which takes more strength: holding on, or letting go? Choose one person who faced that choice: a character from a story you know, or yourself. Name the moment, take a side, and support it with one specific detail. Write 150 to 200 words, an argument, not a summary. Use at least one of this week’s ten words.

📖 Jonah’s draft, a model
Jonah
6th Grade Scholar · the kite

When someone wrongs you, letting go takes more strength than getting even. I know because of what happened to my kite last spring. My grandpa and I built it out of sticks and a red trash bag, and it took us two weekends. My cousin Theo, a seventh grader stepped on it and then laughed about it. The sticks snapped right in the middle. I was so mad that I got the scissors to cut the string on his kite. I stood there with the scissors in my hand for a long time. Then I put them back in the drawer. Getting even would have taken about two seconds. Letting go was laborious. It took the whole afternoon, and I had to keep deciding it every time I saw his kite up in the air. That is why I think letting go is the harder choice. Getting even is fast, but letting go is harder.
